A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PWM and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. The renamed title and reorganized sections can be matched reliably; documentation inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original ball-wall and double-pendulum simulations, five locomotion-task experiments, MT30/MT80 evaluations, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds DreamerV3 locomotion results and Appendix F experiments on regularization, shared policies, and the actor objective.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 corrects the reported updates: v1 adds loss values to parameters, whereas v3 explicitly uses gradient descent for the world model and critic and gradient ascent for the actor. The architecture, objectives in Equations 6–10, and rollout procedure are retained. This is a limited pseudocode correction, without establishing an implementation change.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same toy systems, five dflex locomotion tasks, MT30/MT80 environments, and stiff-contact scenario. Appendix F applies additional analyses and policy configurations to existing tasks; it introduces no new dataset, domain, or environmental test scenario.

E2.justification: DreamerV3, previously included as an MT30 single-task expert, joins the five-task dflex comparison in Figures 5 and 13 and Tables 3–4. Appendix F.2 also adds explicit MT30 comparisons with TD-MPC2 without planning and PWM with a shared policy. These substantially broaden the comparisons supporting the central design choices.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces controlled protocols comparing task-conditioned shared policies on MT30 and replacing PWM's actor objective with TD(lambda) on Hopper, Ant, and Anymal. These are added experimental configurations. The retained benchmark datasets, metrics, training settings, and Table 1 hyperparameters are otherwise unchanged; seed-reporting changes are assessed under E5.

E4.justification: New Appendix F extends the regularization ablation from Ant to Hopper, Anymal, and Humanoid, tests shared versus per-task policies and dependence on planning, and compares actor objectives. These directly investigate previously untested design questions. The four main ablations and Appendix E horizon analysis already existed in v1.

E5.justification: The single-task main text, Figure 13, and Table 3 change their reported seed counts from five to ten. V1's Table 4 already states ten, so an actual doubling of runs cannot be established. IQM, confidence-interval, and standard-deviation reporting practices remain. New Appendix F.1 specifies three seeds, while Figure 17 specifies five.

E6.justification: Tables 3–4 add DreamerV3 results and revise existing scores. For example, Table 4 changes PWM's SNU Humanoid reward from 4585 ± 958 to 5767 ± 2394 and TD-MPC2's Ant reward from 6591 ± 2708 to 7080 ± 2885. Appendix F adds shared-policy failure and actor-objective findings. These are revised or additional results, not established performance gains from a changed method.

T1.justification: V3 Section 3.1 introduces parameter distance, ||theta_hat - theta*||, as the optimality gap. V1 defines it through objective-value difference in Figure 2, and v3 retains that figure's definition, creating a mathematical inconsistency. The principal objectives, assumptions, and derivations otherwise remain; no new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The headline claims concerning 152 action dimensions, 80 tasks, up to 27% higher rewards, and rapid policy extraction remain. V3 adds an explicit introductory claim that decoupling supervised world-model training from per-task RL improves stability and efficiency, sharpening the claimed benefit of the existing framework.

C2.justification: Appendix F newly attributes shared-policy failure to unstable RL optimization and suggests that PWM's actor objective benefits from simpler, less noisy gradients. It also qualifies this preference by noting TD(lambda)'s greater computational cost but potentially steadier Anymal learning and the need for further study. The existing data, adaptation, and world-model-scaling limitations remain.

D1.justification: V3 adds a reproducibility statement advertising training data and checkpoints alongside code, identifying public TD-MPC2 data, and describing simulator licenses. Appendix C's implementation details and Table 1 hyperparameters are substantially unchanged. The PDFs establish these access disclosures, not the external resources' actual availability.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts from broad motivation around large generalist world models toward PWM's relationship to gradient-based simulation methods and shared versus per-task policies. V3 explicitly discusses its relationship to DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2, adds AHAC, MVE, and GATO, and removes the GAIA-1/UniSim motivation and several other references. This exceeds mere relocation or bibliographic updating.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statements, related work, single-task experiment introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, the title changes from large to multi-task world models, and new reproducibility and Appendix F sections alter the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V3 adds Figures 17–19, expands Figures 1, 5, and 13 and Tables 3–4 for DreamerV3, revises Figure 6's timing display, and relocates Algorithm 1 and several displays. The conference template also changes typography and page layout. Existing appendix figures are retained, including the individual MT30/MT80 results.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the empirical justification for PWM by adding the missing DreamerV3 locomotion comparison, directly testing the rationale for separate policies, and extending regularization evidence beyond Ant. Appendix F also tests the actor objective and acknowledges a stability tradeoff. Corrected algorithm updates and expanded reproducibility disclosures improve usability. The new optimality-gap inconsistency and conflicting ablation seed counts limit precision, but do not outweigh the stronger evidence for central design choices.
